target: छात्रों को नई वर्दी दी गई है।
english: Students have been given new uniforms.
tip: English makes 'students' the subject of 'were given'. Hindi doesn't: छात्रों को (chhatron ko = to the students) stays, and दी गई (di gai) agrees with वर्दी (vardi = uniform).

target: स्कूल में नई लाइब्रेरी बनी है।
english: A new library has been built at the school.
tip: बनी है (bani hai) is not a passive – it's बनना (banna = to get made). Hindi often says 'the library became' where English needs 'was built', no जाना (jana) involved.

target: गंगा को भारत की सबसे पवित्र नदी मानते हैं।
english: Ganga is considered India's holiest river.
tip: No one says who considers: मानते हैं (maante hain = [people] consider) has no subject at all. Where English says 'is considered', Hindi often just drops the 'they'.

target: अपराधी को उम्रक़ैद की सज़ा सुनाई गई।
english: The criminal was sentenced to life imprisonment.
tip: A sentence is announced aloud in Hindi: सज़ा सुनाई गई (saza sunai gai) is literally 'the punishment was made heard' – सुनाना (sunana) means to make someone hear.

target: मुग़लों ने इस क़िले को बनवाया था।
english: The Mughals built this fort.
tip: बनवाया (banvaya) is not plain 'built' – the -वा- (-va-) means the Mughals had it built by others. बनाया (banaya) = built it yourself; बनवाया = got it built.

target: इस रास्ते पर भारी गाड़ियों को जाने से मना है।
english: Heavy vehicles are not allowed on this road.
tip: जाने से मना है (jane se mana hai) is literally 'there is refusal from going' – the banned action takes से (se = from). That's the standard 'not allowed' pattern on signs.

target: मैंने आज बैंक से पैसे निकाले।
english: I withdrew money from the bank today.
tip: Completed actions mark the doer with ने: मैंने (maine = I). The verb then agrees with the object – निकाले (nikaale) is plural for पैसे (paise = money), not for 'I'.

target: उदास बच्ची ने गुड़िया को गले लगाया।
english: The sad girl hugged the doll.
tip: Hugging is neck-based: गले लगाया (gale lagaya) is literally 'attached to the neck'. गला (gala) means the neck-throat area – that's where the hug happens.

target: सभी छात्रों ने परीक्षा दी।
english: All students took the exam.
tip: You give an exam in Hindi to take it: परीक्षा दी (pariksha di = gave the exam). The examiner is the one who takes it – परीक्षा ली (pariksha li). Reversed from English.

target: दादाजी ने मुझे गोटी से कैरम खेलना सिखाया।
english: Grandfather taught me how to play carrom with pieces.
tip: Adding जी (ji) shows respect or warmth: दादाजी (dadaji = respected grandfather). Elders often get it built in – पिताजी (pitaji), माताजी (mataji).

target: गीता हर महीने अपने पैसे बचाती है।
english: Geeta saves her money every month.
tip: No ने (ne) here – बचाती है (bachati hai = saves) is a habit, and ने only marks completed past actions. Present-tense doers stay plain: गीता (Geeta), not गीता ने.

target: ममता बिना कुछ कहे कमरे से बाहर चली गई।
english: Mamta left the room without saying a word.
tip: Even in the past, ने (ne) skips motion verbs: चली गई (chali gayi = went off) takes no ने. Only verbs that act on an object use it.

target: मैंने ऑनलाइन ट्रेन का टिकट बुक किया।
english: I booked the train ticket online.
tip: English words become Hindi verbs through किया (kiya = did): बुक किया (book kiya) = booked. Same pattern for फ़ोन किया (phone kiya) and ऑर्डर किया (order kiya).

target: मैंने आज बिजली का बिल भर दिया।
english: I paid the electricity bill today.
tip: Bills get filled, not paid: बिल भर दिया (bill bhar diya = filled the bill). भरना (bharna = to fill) covers paying bills, fees and fines.

target: दीदी ने मेरे लिए खाना गरम कर दिया।
english: My sister heated up the food for me.
tip: Adding दिया (diya = gave) to a verb means done for someone else: गरम कर दिया (garam kar diya) – heated it for me. With लिया (liya = took) it would be for herself.

target: टिकट कहाँ से मिलेगा?
english: Where can I get the ticket?
tip: Hindi skips 'get' – things turn up instead: मिलेगा (milega = will be found). You ask where the ticket will be found, not where you can get it.

target: रात तक बारिश रुक जाएगी।
english: The rain will stop by night.
tip: रुक जाएगी (ruk jaayegi) adds जाना (jaana = to go) to 'stop' – the go-verb marks a complete change: the rain won't just pause, it will stop for good.

target: अगले महीने नई दुकान खुलेगी।
english: A new shop will open next month.
tip: Future verbs carry gender: दुकान (dukaan = shop) is feminine, so it खुलेगी (khulegi), ending in -egi. A masculine subject would take खुलेगा (khulega).

target: अरे भाई, आज बाज़ार चलोगे?
english: Hey brother, will you go to the market today?
tip: चलोगे (chaloge) is an invite: चलना (chalna) means going along together, so this asks 'coming to the market with me?' Going on your own is जाना (jaana).

target: क्या आप एक कप चाय लेंगे?
english: Would you like a cup of tea?
tip: Polite offers use 'take', not 'have': चाय लेंगे? (chaay lenge? = will you take tea?). Future + लेना (lena) is the standard courteous way to offer.

target: डेढ़ घंटे में हम पहुँच जाएँगे।
english: We will reach in one and a half hours.
tip: डेढ़ (dedh) is one word meaning exactly 'one and a half' – Hindi gives 1.5 and 2.5 their own words (ढाई / dhaai = 2.5) rather than phrases.

target: डॉक्टर दस मिनट में आपको देखेंगे।
english: The doctor will see you in ten minutes.
tip: One doctor, plural verb: देखेंगे (dekhenge) is the respectful plural. Singular देखेगा (dekhega) here would sound rude – respect makes one person grammatically plural.

target: चौराहे पर बाएँ मुड़ने के बाद अस्पताल आएगा।
english: After turning left at the intersection, you will find the hospital.
tip: In Hindi directions, landmarks come to you: अस्पताल आएगा (aspataal aayega = the hospital will come). You don't find it – after the turn, it shows up.

target: जितनी मेहनत करोगे, उतना फल मिलेगा।
english: The more you work, the more reward you will get.
tip: 'The more... the more' needs a matched pair: जितनी मेहनत करोगे (jitni mehnat karoge), उतना फल मिलेगा (utna phal milega) – jitni sets it up, utna answers it.

target: अगर मौसम अच्छा रहा, तो हम पिकनिक पर चलेंगे।
english: If the weather is good, we will go on a picnic.
tip: The if-half of a future condition uses a past form: अगर मौसम अच्छा रहा (agar mausam achchha raha = if the weather stayed good). Only चलेंगे (chalenge) is future.

target: मैं तुम्हें फ़ोटो बाद में भेज दूँगा।
english: I'll send you the photos later.
tip: भेज दूँगा (bhej doonga) adds देना (dena = to give) to 'send' – the give-helper marks doing it for someone else, a favor tone plain भेजूँगा (bhejoonga) lacks.

target: जिज्ञासु छात्र ने शिक्षक से सवाल पूछा।
english: The curious student asked the teacher a question.
tip: You ask FROM someone in Hindi – शिक्षक से सवाल पूछा (shikshak se sawaal poochha): से (se = from) marks the person asked, not को (ko).

target: वंदना ने न सिर्फ़ परीक्षा पास की बल्कि पहला नंबर भी पाया।
english: Vandana not only passed the exam but also got first place.
tip: In न सिर्फ़...बल्कि (na sirf...balki = not only...but rather), the 'also' splits off – भी (bhi) lands after the new item: पहला नंबर भी (pahla number bhi).

target: चूँकि बारिश हो रही थी, इसलिए हम घर पर ही रुके।
english: Since it was raining, we stayed home.
tip: To lead with the reason, use चूँकि (choonki = since), answered by इसलिए (isliye = so): चूँकि बारिश हो रही थी, इसलिए... क्योंकि (kyonki = because) usually follows the main clause instead.

target: मैंने अलार्म लगाया ताकि सुबह जल्दी उठ सकूँ।
english: I set an alarm so that I can wake up early.
tip: After ताकि (taaki = so that), the verb takes its wish form – उठ सकूँ (uth sakoon), not the plain future उठूँगा (uthoonga).
